H1.text: A kite tugs on its string. A box scrapes across the floor. A kicked ball flies. Each has several forces on it at once.

H2.text: To untangle them, physicists use one simple drawing.

H3.text: Aarav drags a box of books down the corridor, with a rope.

H4.text: The box speeds up. How many forces act on it? Most people say one, his pull. The answer is four.

H5.text: Let's find all four, with a free-body diagram.

P1.text: A free-body diagram shows one body, cut free from everything around it.

P2.text: We draw the body as a box, and every force on it as an arrow.

P3.text: Only forces on the body. Never forces it exerts on others.

P4.text: Then we add the forces along each direction, and use the second law.

S1.text: To the motion notebook. A two kilogram block on a rough floor, with a rope tied to it.

S2.text: First, isolate the block. Everything else fades.

S3.text: Force one: its weight, straight down. m g, two times nine point eight, nineteen point six newtons.

S4.text: Force two: the floor pushes up. The normal force, also nineteen point six, since the block does not move up or down.

S5.text: Force three: the rope pulls it forward. The tension, ten newtons.

S6.text: Force four: friction from the floor, pulling back. Six newtons while it slides.

S7.text: Up and down, they cancel. Along the floor, ten minus six leaves four newtons. a is four over two, two metres per second squared.

S8.text: Pull harder. Fourteen newtons gives four. Eighteen gives six.

S9.text: On the graph, the dots sit on a straight line. Its slope is one over the mass.

S10.text: Slow-mo replay. Freeze, and check every arrow.

S11.text: Four forces. The block's own push on the floor is not here. It acts on the floor.

S12.text: Your turn. The rope snaps. Which forces act on the block as it slides on? Pause and decide.

S13.text: Weight, normal force and friction! No force of motion. Friction alone acts along the floor, so the block slows and stops.

D1.text: Now the method, one step at a time.

D2.text: Step one. Pick one body, and draw it alone.

D3.text: Step two. Draw every force on it. Weight first, then one for each thing touching it.

D4.text: Step three. Choose axes: x along the motion, y across it.

D5.text: Step four. Along y, there is no acceleration. So N minus m g is zero. N equals m g.

D6.text: Step five. Along x, the sum of the forces equals m a. So T minus f equals m a.

T1.text: Remember this. Draw only the forces on the body, then add them along each axis.

R1.text: Here is a test for every arrow. Link by link.

R2.text: Each force needs a giver. The weight? The Earth pulls.

R3.text: The normal force and friction? The floor, where it touches.

R5.text: No giver? Then no force. That is why there is no force of motion.

K1.text: Side by side. Left: forces on the block, from the Earth, the floor and the rope. They go in its diagram.

K2.text: Right: the forces by the block. It presses the floor, pulls the rope, and pulls the Earth. They belong to other diagrams.

K3.text: Now you try. A kicked ball flies through the air. Ignore air. Which forces are on its diagram? Pause and decide.

K4.text: Weight only! The foot no longer touches the ball. Only the Earth still pulls on it.

W2.text: Aarav lifts a five kilogram box with a rope, speeding it up at two metres per second squared. Find the tension.

W3.text: Two forces: tension up, weight down. The weight is five times nine point eight, forty nine newtons.

W5.text: Up is positive. T minus forty nine equals five times two.

W6.text: So T is fifty nine newtons. More than the weight, because the box speeds up as it rises.

X2.text: Many students add the block's push on the floor to its own diagram.

X3.text: But that force acts on the floor. The diagram holds only forces on the body.

E1.text: Where is this asked? In almost every laws of motion numerical: blocks, ropes, pulleys and lifts.

Q1.text: Exam level now. A four kilogram block on a smooth floor is pulled by a rope with twenty newtons, at thirty seven degrees above the horizontal. Sine thirty seven is point six, and g is ten. Find the normal force and the acceleration. Pause and solve.

A1.text: The answer is B. Twenty eight newtons, and four metres per second squared.

A2.text: Three forces: weight forty down, the normal force up, and the rope's twenty newtons at thirty seven degrees.

A3.text: Along y: N plus twenty times point six equals forty. N is twenty eight newtons.

A4.text: Along x: cos thirty seven is point eight. Twenty times point eight is sixteen. Over four kilograms, four metres per second squared.

F1.text: Here is your recap. Screenshot this card.

Y1.text: Can you answer these without help?

Y2.text: One. How many forces act on Aarav's box, and who gives each one?

Y3.text: Two. Why is the block's push on the floor left out of its diagram?

Y4.text: Three. A box speeds up as it rises. Why is the tension more than its weight?

N1.text: Next time: Aarav hangs his bag on a rope. He pulls it tight, but it always sags. Why? Equilibrium of forces.
